It is designed to streamline and accelerate the end-to-end hiring process for companies of all sizes — from startups to enterprises — by automating candidate screening, interviewing, and pipeline management using artificial intelligence. The platform promises a 10x faster hiring cycle and 5x return on investment by replacing manual screening with AI-driven workflows, reducing time-to-hire from weeks to 48–72 hours for a qualified shortlist. Next.js Code Review Model — Architecture Plan — March 2026
Architecture Planning Document
A Compact Discriminative Code Review Model Specialised for Next.js
Project type
Research proposal — model design and training plan
Focus domain
Next.js App Router (TypeScript / React Server Components)
Model family
Discriminative encoder (CodeBERT / GraphCodeBERT) + LoRA
Date
March 2026
ABSTRACT
This document presents the complete architectural plan for a compact, locally deployable
discriminative model for automated code review, specialised for the Next.js framework. The system
fine-tunes a CodeBERT or GraphCodeBERT encoder using LoRA on a curated dataset of real GitHub pull
request diffs, producing four simultaneous outputs: multi-label issue category classification, a quality
score, a severity rating, and line-level issue localisation. The quantised model is approximately 50 MB
and runs at sub-150ms inference on CPU only — requiring no internet connection, no cloud service, and
no GPU. The document covers input design, encoder architecture, multi-task training, dataset
construction, evaluation strategy, and deployment tooling across nine planned project phases.
Keywords: automated code review · discriminative classification · CodeBERT · LoRA fine-tuning · Next.js · multi-task
learning · local deployment

Architecture Planning — Next.js Discriminative Code Review Model
p. 2
Next.js Code Review Model — Architecture Plan — March 2026
1   System Overview
End-to-end pipeline from data collection to deployed developer tool
The system is structured as a single pre-trained transformer encoder fine-tuned on
domain-specific data, with all inference running on the developer's local machine. No code leaves
the local environment. Figure 1 shows the complete pipeline across six stages.
Figure 1. End-to-end pipeline: GitHub PR data collection � input construction � CodeBERT encoder � LoRA fine-tuning �
 task heads � ONNX deployment.
 
The six pipeline stages are: (1) collecting real pull request diffs and inline reviewer comments from
high-activity Next.js repositories via the GitHub REST API; (2) constructing the tokenised input
sequence by concatenating the file path, diff, and surrounding file context; (3) encoding the
sequence through the pre-trained CodeBERT or GraphCodeBERT transformer; (4) applying LoRA
adapters to the upper transformer layers during fine-tuning; (5) routing encoder outputs to four
task-specific heads; and (6) exporting to ONNX with 4-bit quantisation for local deployment.
2   Input Representation
Token sequence construction, segment embeddings, 512-token budget
The input encodes three complementary information sources: the file path, the code diff, and
surrounding file context. For Next.js specifically, file context is not optional — whether a
component is a Server or Client Component is determined by the 'use client' directive at the file
top, which does not appear in a diff of a changed function within that file.

2.1  Token sequence structure
The sequence follows the BERT two-segment format: [CLS] [SEP] [SEP]. The [CLS] token
produces the aggregate representation consumed by the three document-level heads. Per-token
representations feed the line-level head. The 512-token budget is allocated as: file path (fewer than
10 tokens), diff (up to 350 tokens), and context (approximately 30 surrounding lines). Over 92% of
TypeScript diffs in the target repositories fit without truncation.

3   Encoder Architecture and LoRA Fine-tuning
12-layer RoBERTa encoder, layer-freezing strategy, rank-8 adapters
The encoder backbone is either CodeBERT or GraphCodeBERT — both RoBERTa-based
architectures with 12 transformer layers, 12 self-attention heads, a 768-d hidden dimension, and
approximately 125 million parameters. They differ in pre-training: CodeBERT uses masked
language modelling on NL-PL pairs; GraphCodeBERT additionally incorporates data flow graphs,
giving it stronger structural code understanding for tasks requiring variable dependency
reasoning.

Architecture Planning — Next.js Discriminative Code Review Model
p. 4
Next.js Code Review Model — Architecture Plan — March 2026
Figure 3. Encoder internals with LoRA and task heads. Layers 1-8 are frozen; layers 9-12 receive rank-8 LoRA adapters
 on W_q and W_v. The [CLS] token drives three sequence-level heads; all token vectors drive the line-level
 classification head.
 
3.1  Layer-freezing strategy
Research by Shi et al. (2023) established that lower transformer layers encode general syntactic
code properties while upper layers encode semantic, task-specific features. Layers 1-8 are
therefore frozen during fine-tuning and layers 9-12 receive LoRA adapters. This reduces trainable
parameters from 125M to approximately 300K — less than 0.25% of total parameters — while
preserving the general code understanding acquired during pre-training on hundreds of millions
of code-text pairs.
3.2  LoRA adapter configuration
rank (r)         : 8
alpha (scaling)  : 16
target modules   : q_proj, v_proj  (attention only)
layers           : 9, 10, 11, 12  (upper 4 of 12)
trainable params : 4 layers x 2 matrices x 2 x (768 x 8)  =  196,608
initialisation   : A ~ N(0, sigma),  B = 0  (zero initial perturbation)

With rank r=8 and hidden dimension d=768, each LoRA adapter contributes 2 x 768 x 8 = 12,288
parameters per layer. Applied to Q and V weight matrices in the top four layers, the total LoRA
overhead is 196,608 parameters — less than 0.16% of the base model size. The zero initialisation of
matrix B ensures the model begins fine-tuning exactly at the pre-trained checkpoint with no initial
perturbation.

activation — shallow by design to keep inference fast.

4.1  Combined training objective
L_total = w1 * L_category  +  w2 * L_quality  +  w3 * L_severity  +  w4 * L_lines
Initial weights  : w1 = w2 = w3 = w4 = 1.0

WHY MULTI-TASK LEARNING HELPS HERE
Issue category, severity, and quality are correlated signals. A security issue is
almost always critical; a naming issue is almost invariably informational. Training all
heads simultaneously forces the shared encoder to build representations that capture
these correlations, improving performance on each individual head beyond what
single-task fine-tuning achieves — especially for low-frequency categories where
training data is scarce.
5   Dataset Construction
GitHub PR collection, filtering, label extraction, splitting

Architecture Planning — Next.js Discriminative Code Review Model
p. 7
Next.js Code Review Model — Architecture Plan — March 2026
Figure 4. Dataset construction and labelling pipeline. Source repositories are queried via the GitHub REST API; raw PR
data is filtered; labels are extracted from inline reviewer comments; the dataset is split by PR to prevent leakage.
5.1  Collection and filtering
Closed pull requests are retrieved using GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=closed. Per PR:
the diff (Accept: application/vnd.github.v3.diff) and inline comments (GET
/pulls/{pull_number}/comments). Inclusion criteria: only .ts and .tsx diffs; comment body length
>= 40 characters; comment author type != Bot; comment body does not match /^(LGTM|looks
good|nit:)/i; diff contains at least 3 changed lines. Target: 20,000-30,000 raw samples yielding
15,000-20,000 after filtering.
5.2  Label extraction
Labels are extracted in two passes. Pass 1 applies deterministic keyword patterns (e.g.
'useCallback', 're-render' -> performance; 'exposed', 'sanitize' -> security; 'Server Component', 'App
Router' -> nextjs-pattern). Pass 2 sends unmatched samples to GPT-4o with a structured
JSON-output prompt. A 10% random sample of all auto-labelled examples is manually verified to
establish label reliability before training begins.
5.3  Train / validation / test split
The dataset is split at the PR level (not the comment level) using an 80/10/10 ratio. Splitting by PR
prevents data leakage: comments from the same PR share diff context and reviewer style, so
placing them across splits would inflate test performance unrealistically. Stratified sampling is
used to ensure each split preserves the overall class distribution across all eight issue categories.

7   Local Deployment Architecture
ONNX export, quantisation, VS Code / CLI / pre-commit integration
Figure 6. Deployment architecture. The quantised ONNX model is loaded by the ONNX Runtime and exposed through
 three integration points. Sample output shows line-level annotations.
 
The trained model is exported to ONNX format with 4-bit dynamic quantisation, reducing the file
from approximately 130 MB (float32) to approximately 50 MB (int4). ONNX Runtime handles CPU
inference at sub-150ms per diff on standard developer hardware. Three integration modes are
planned:
VS Code Extension
Integrates with the VS Code Diagnostics API. Surfaces inline annotations as
yellow (warning) or red (critical) markers on changed lines whenever a
TypeScript file is saved.
CLI tool npx
nextreview
Scans a directory and produces a structured JSON report or human-readable
console output. Can be piped into other tools.
Pre-commit hook
Runs on staged diffs before each commit. Blocks the commit if any critical
issues are detected; lists flagged lines with category and confidence score.
8   Evaluation Framework
Automatic metrics, human evaluation, ablation design

Architecture Planning — Next.js Discriminative Code Review Model
p. 10
Next.js Code Review Model — Architecture Plan — March 2026
 Figure 7. Evaluation framework with three pillars and four baselines.
 
Evaluation is structured across three complementary pillars. Automatic metrics provide objective
comparison against baselines. Human evaluation establishes real-world validity with practising
developers. Ablation studies attribute performance to specific architectural choices.
8.1  Automatic metrics
For the category head: per-class F1, precision, recall; macro and micro-averaged F1; AUC-ROC per
category. For the quality regression head: MSE and Pearson correlation. For severity: accuracy and
weighted F1. For the line-level head: Top-5 and Top-10 accuracy, following the evaluation
methodology of LineVul (Fu & Tantithamthavorn, MSR 2022).
8.2  Human evaluation protocol
A stratified sample of 100 diffs is drawn from the held-out test set and presented to three
independent Next.js developers with 3+ years of experience. Each rates the model output on a
5-point Likert scale across three dimensions: correctness, actionability, and localisation
specificity. Fleiss' kappa measures inter-rater agreement. The same 100 diffs are also evaluated by
ESLint and GPT-4o for direct comparison.

Abstract
Automated code review (ACR) has advanced considerably through the application of

cloud-dependent, and trained on generic multi-language corpora that inadequately

and multi-task learning — to establish the theoretical and empirical foundations for a
compact, discriminative code review model specifically designed for Next.js. The review
identifies a clear gap at the intersection of framework-specialised review, discriminative
multi-task architectures, and local deployment constraints, and articulates four concrete

1. Introduction: The Code Review Problem
Code review — the systematic inspection of source code by one or more developers
prior to integration into a production codebase — is among the most widely adopted
quality assurance practices in modern software engineering. Empirical evidence
consistently demonstrates its value: reviewed code exhibits lower defect rates,
higher internal quality, and is generally easier to comprehend and maintain
(Bacchelli & Bird, 2013; McIntosh et al., 2014; Morales et al., 2015). Bavota & Russo,
2015 found that unreviewed code introduces bugs at more than twice the rate of
reviewed code, a finding that has been corroborated across multiple industrial and
open-source contexts.
Despite its benefits, code review imposes a substantial and often underestimated
cost. With more than 28 million software developers globally spending between 10
and 20 percent of their working time on review tasks, the aggregate demand
exceeds 22 million developer hours every day. The landmark study by Bacchelli &
Bird (ICSE 2013), which surveyed 873 programmers and 165 managers across
Microsoft, found that while defect detection is the primary stated motivation for
code review, its actual outcomes are considerably broader — encompassing
knowledge transfer, team awareness, and the proposal of alternative design
solutions. This gap between expected and actual outcomes suggests that human

The challenge is further compounded by the specificity of modern frameworks.
Next.js, currently the fourth most popular web framework according to the Stack

creating new categories of defect — including accidental data exposure, incorrect

implementations — that have no direct analogue in prior frameworks. No existing
automated code review system is trained to recognise or classify these patterns.
This is the primary motivation and gap this research addresses.
Research gap
Existing ACR systems are generative, cloud-dependent, or trained on generic
multi-language corpora. No compact, discriminative, locally deployable model
exists that is specialised for the semantic patterns of the Next.js App Router. This

2. Automated Code Review: History and State of the Art
Research into automated support for code review can be traced across three
broadly distinct generations, distinguished by their underlying methodology and the
scope of review tasks they address.
2.1 First generation: Static analysis and rule-based systems
The earliest automated code review tools operated through static analysis —
exhaustive enumeration of syntactic and stylistic rules against which source code is
checked without execution. Tools such as Checkstyle, FindBugs, and ESLint
represent this approach, as does the FindBugs-based ReviewBot system
(Balachandran, 2013) which integrated static analysis into the Gerrit code review
platform. As noted by Singh et al. (2017), static analysis tools provide precise,
reproducible feedback on well-defined rule violations but are fundamentally

Discriminative Code Analysis for Automated Review Literature Review 3 incapable of reasoning about context, semantics, or intent. A rule engine cannot determine that a particular use of fetch() without a cache directive is problematic specifically because the enclosing component is a Next.js Server Component — such reasoning requires understanding of both the code and its execution environment. Additionally, most code review platforms — including Gerrit, Phabricator, and Code Flow — provide only basic automation support and do not reduce reviewers' burden in a meaningful way (Tymchuk et al., 2015; Pascarella et al., 2018). This gap between the available tooling and the needs of modern development teams motivated the transition to learning-based approaches. 2.2 Second generation: Neural machine translation models The second generation of ACR systems reframed code review as a machine translation problem — specifically, treating the transformation of a code diff into either a reviewer comment or a corrected code version as a sequence-to-sequence learning task. Tufano et al. (ICSE 2021) were among the first to frame both the contributor and reviewer perspectives of code review as neural machine translation tasks, using Transformer architectures trained on real GitHub pull request data. Their work established the foundational insight that reviewer comments and code diffs constitute naturally paired training data, making large-scale supervised learning feasible without manual annotation. DeepReview (Lo, PAKDD 2019) introduced multi-instance learning for review classification, providing an early demonstration that discriminative models — models that predict a class rather than generate text — could be trained on review corpora with meaningful accuracy. 4. Code Classification and Defect Detection
The multi-label issue category head at the core of the proposed architecture is an
instance of the broader family of code classification problems, for which a
substantial and mature body of empirical evidence exists. This section surveys the
most directly relevant results, from function-level defect detection to fine-grained
line-level prediction.
4.1 Function-level defect and vulnerability detection
The CodeXGLUE benchmark (Lu et al., NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks, 2021)
established a standard evaluation suite for code intelligence tasks, including defect

Discriminative Code Analysis for Automated Review Literature Review 7 detection. Research combining graph neural networks with pre-trained transformer encoders for software defect detection on the CodeXGLUE Defect sub-task achieves F1-scores of up to 91.7%, representing a 23.6-point absolute improvement over LSTM-based baselines — demonstrating that pre-trained transformer encoders substantially outperform earlier sequence models on code classification. For the more specific task of vulnerability detection, the contrastive learning approach SCL-CVD (Wang et al., Computers & Security, 2024) fine-tunes GraphCodeBERT using LoRA on three widely used benchmark datasets — Devign, Reveal, and Big-Vul — and reports a relative improvement of 35.68% over all baselines, including vanilla CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT fine-tuned with standard cross-entropy loss. The paper attributes this improvement to the contrastive objective's ability to separate the representations of vulnerable and non-vulnerable samples in the embedding space, which is particularly effective when the two classes are superficially similar — a characteristic shared by the issue categories targeted in this work, where a correctly structured Server Component and one with a subtle cache misconfiguration are lexically nearly identical. 4.2 Multi-label classification for code quality The issue category head proposed here produces multi-label outputs: a single diff may receive multiple category labels simultaneously. This differs from the binary classification setting of most defect detection research. The technical approach is well-established: replacing the binary sigmoid output of a standard classifier with a multi-label sigmoid head trained with binary cross-entropy loss per class, with a shared encoder whose [CLS] token representation serves as the aggregate code representation. This formulation is identical to that used in multi-label text classification tasks in NLP, and has been demonstrated to transfer effectively to code classification settings with code-aware encoders (CodeXGLUE, Lu et al., 2021). A key practical challenge in multi-label code classification is class imbalance: issues such as security vulnerabilities are rare compared to naming or performance issues. Research on vulnerability detection consistently identifies imbalance as a critical factor (Cheshkov et al., ICCQ 2024), and prior work recommends focal loss or sample weighting strategies to address this. Crucially, the performance gains are largest on tasks with smaller datasets — directly relevant for this project, where training data for rare issue categories (e.g., security) will be scarcer than for common ones (e.g., naming). The theoretical basis for this behaviour is the regularisation effect of multi-task learning: because the shared encoder must simultaneously represent useful features for multiple tasks, it is prevented from overfitting to idiosyncrasies of any single task's training distribution. As Caruana (1997) originally characterised it, multi-task learning uses the domain information contained in related tasks' training signals as an inductive bias, improving generalisation by learning tasks in parallel while sharing representation. For the present work, issue category, severity, and quality score are strongly correlated signals: a security issue is almost always critical, while a naming issue is almost invariably informational. Learning these joint distributions produces shared representations that are more discriminative for each individual task than single-task fine-tuning would achieve. 5.2 Negative transfer and task weighting Multi-task learning does not unconditionally improve performance. When the gradients of different tasks conflict — pointing in opposing directions or differing significantly in magnitude — joint training can hinder individual task performance, a phenomenon known as negative transfer (Wikipedia, Multi-task learning; Chen et al., Semantic Scholar 2021). For the proposed architecture, the risk of negative transfer is low because the four tasks are genuinely correlated: all operate on the same input (code diff + context), and their outputs (category, severity, quality, line location) are jointly determined by the same underlying properties of the code change. Nonetheless, the training objective must weight task losses appropriately: The combined training loss is defined as L = w1*L_cat + w2*L_quality + w3*L_severity + w4*L_lines, where w1, w2, w3, w4 are task weights and L_cat, L_quality, L_severity, and L_lines are the per-task losses. Initial experiments will use equal weights (all w = 1.0), followed by grid search to identify the optimal balance. 6.1 Empirical evidence for context-enriched representations
A study presented at MSR 2024 found that encoding structural context and version
history alongside source code improves code classification model performance
across five pre-trained architectures — including CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT —
with contextual signals providing consistent gains beyond what static code
snapshots alone can achieve. While that work focused primarily on file-level
structural context and commit history, the principle generalises: models that
observe more of the execution environment in which code operates make better
classification decisions.
The technical basis for this approach is the BERT sentence-pair input format, in
which the [CLS] token aggregates information from both segments through
bidirectional self-attention. This enables the encoder to learn joint representations
of the diff and its surrounding context simultaneously, rather than processing them
independently and fusing them post-hoc. The 512-token input limit of
CodeBERT/GraphCodeBERT constrains the amount of context that can be
incorporated; the proposed approach uses 30 lines around changed lines, which
empirically fits within the token budget for the majority of TypeScript function
bodies.

7.1 Synthesis of the identified gap
The literature reviewed above establishes five independently supported propositions
that together define the research gap this work addresses:

From P1–P5, the gap follows directly: an architecture satisfying P2–P4 and trained on
data capturing P5 does not yet exist. Existing systems satisfy at most three of the

P1 and P2 but are generative, cloud-dependent, and framework-generic. No existing
system satisfies all five simultaneously.

8. Conclusion
This literature review has surveyed four areas of directly relevant prior work —
automated code review systems, pre-trained code language models, code
classification and defect detection, and multi-task learning — and established the
theoretical and empirical foundations for the proposed research. The review
demonstrates that all component techniques are individually well-validated:
discriminative code classification with CodeBERT achieves F1 scores above 0.91 on
established benchmarks; multi-task learning with shared encoders consistently
improves over single-task baselines, especially in limited-data regimes; line-level
prediction is tractable with transformer-based token classification heads; and
context-enriched input representations improve code classification accuracy across
a range of pre-trained architectures.
The gap identified by this review is not merely an absence of prior work but a
principled confluence: the existing literature has not combined these techniques in a
locally deployable, framework-specialised discriminative architecture. Next.js in
particular represents an underexplored but high-value target domain whose specific
patterns — Server Components, App Router semantics, caching directives, and
Server Actions — are semantically distinct from prior-art training corpora and
require dedicated treatment. The four contributions proposed in this research
directly address this gap, and the technical feasibility of each contribution is
well-supported by the reviewed literature.
